tn.quote: PaTani has two distinctive tones: high and low. The following minimal pairs show that tone is phonemic in PaTani. The high tone is represented here by "1" and the low tone is represented by "2". ... PaTani has a word-tone pattern, where in polysyllabic morphemes only the first vowel has contrastive tone and subsequent syllable(s) have levelled tone, i.e. if the first syllable has a high tone, then subsequent vowels have slightly lower pitch; and if the first syllable has a low tone, then subsequent vowels have slightly mid pitch.

SIL OPD 2011 p. 3, under the heading 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)', says only 'Tone is phonemic. Examples: sú [su] tooth, su [su] ginger, suú [su] road' and marks high tone with an acute only when needed. MacDonald 1973: 130-131, summarising Trefry, gives Pawaia 'A high-low tone system exists, and either tone may occur on all vowels'; its two uses of 'stress' (p. 117 on the name Kewa, p. 131 on Witu) do not concern Pawaia. 4540.prule: Stress is not phonemic. One phrase stress per phonological phrase (the stretch between final juncture /#/ and non-final juncture //): on the last syllable of the phrase if it is long ((C)VV), otherwise on the penultimate syllable; in final phrases only voiced syllables count, since a short vowel before final juncture is frequently devoiced. Any other position marks contrastive emphasis. No word-level stress rule is stated; non-final words in a phrase carry no phrase stress (e.g. [#kua+noho+ia+ki+te+táane//]).
4540.srule: Yasuda's 'syllable stress' (non-primary prominence): every syllable is stressed except a short (C)V syllable immediately before any juncture (/#/, // or +); among stressed syllables a long (C)VV syllable is louder than a short one, and /a/ louder than /e o/, louder than /i u/. A graded prominence over the juncture-bounded stretch, not an alternating or word-level secondary stress; no rhythmic secondary stress is described.

4545.prule: Lexical pitch accent, one per phonological word, borne by a single vocalic mora (short vowel, or first or second mora of a long vowel: high level/falling on short V, rising or falling on long V). Minimal pairs by accent position/mora (káti 'saddle' vs katí 'how many?', čúur/čuúr, séeti/seetí). No computable fixed position: the source says placement 'is not entirely predictable' and 'must be defined as lexical'.

tn.quote: De taal der Apende, het Kiphendé heeft twee grondtonen: een gelijkmatige hoge en lage toon. Het toonsysteem is „syllabisch-stationnair” en behoort tot het etymologisch type. De monosyllabische stammen vallen uiteen in twee toongroepen naargelang op de kern een hoge of lage grondtoon rust. De toongroepen of in feite voorkomende combinaties van grondtonen bij de tweeklankgrepen tellende stammen, zijn vier in getal: IA laag-laag, IB laag-hoog, IIA hoog-laag en IIB hoog-hoog. Het prefix heeft in onbeïnvloede positie een lage toon.
tn.translation: The language of the Apende, Kiphendé, has two basic tones: a level high and a low tone. The tone system is 'syllabic-stationary' and belongs to the etymological type. The monosyllabic stems fall into two tone groups according to whether a high or a low basic tone rests on the nucleus. The tone groups, i.e. the actually occurring combinations of basic tones in stems of two syllables, are four in number: IA low-low, IB low-high, IIA high-low and IIB high-high. The prefix has a low tone in uninfluenced position.
tn.cite: Stappers, Leo (1953). De toongroepen en hun wijzigingen in de taal van de Aphende. Kongo-Overzee 19(4): 376-379.
tn.note: Two level tones, high and low, one per syllable; stems fall into lexical tone groups (H/L; LL, LH, HL, HH), noun prefix low; tone patterns change with syntactic construction. Nothing on stress. 4547.exq_: No stress rule, so no stress exceptions. Tonal gap: 'Syllables ending with /ʔ/, however, show no tonal contrast.' (p. 19); 'Tone /31/ is somewhat unusual with stopped syllables, but not unknown' (p. 19).
4547.tone: Three lexical tones /55/ /33/ /31/ (Burling & Phom 1998 pp. 19-20; Bano 2008 §5.10 pp. 168-171 'In Phom language, tones are phonemic... There are three register tones in Phom'; Phom 2018 acoustic confirmation, three tones, 'It was observed that tone sandhi is not present in Phom', ch. 5 p. 110). Glottal-final syllables show no tonal contrast. Neither 'stress' nor 'accent' as a prosodic property of Phom occurs in Burling & Phom (full-text search of the scanned scan: only 'strongly accented' in an English-vowel comparison p. 16 and 'accents over the vowels' as a tone-marking remark p. 21). Bano 2008 lists 'Stress' only as a Chomsky-Halle prosodic feature category (§5.9.3 p. 165) never applied to Phom, plus 'final unstressed vowel schwa' in an apocope rule (p. 185); her tone-placement remark (p. 168): 'In bi-syllabic and tri-syllabic words, the high tones are usually marked on the second syllable, but if the second syllable is followed by a glottal stop, the tone is marked on the first syllables of the words.' Phom 2018 names 'the effect of the stress plays on the tone' as an objective (ch. 5 p. 104) but reports no finding; one offhand line: consonant clusters in derived words 'are pronounced with the same amount of stress as different syllables' (ch. 1 §1.6 p. 30). No source asserts or denies word stress, so tone or pitch accent rather than no word stress.

4549.heavy: Placement of strong stress is quantity-insensitive (always final); syllable structure governs only the degree of non-final prominence (full CV(C)ᵀ = weakly stressed vs. short open CVᵀ presyllable = unstressed) and the fact that a CVᵀ syllable never bears strong stress, which the source states as the restriction 'with all types of syllabic structure except CVᵀ' (i.e. CVᵀ presyllables do not occur word-finally).
4549.prule: Strong (primary) stress falls on the last syllable of every word; monosyllables carry it on their only syllable. Non-contrastive and fully predictable (no stress mark written). Patterns listed: disyllables US, WS; trisyllables WUS, WWS; quadrisyllables UWUS, UWWS, WWWS, all ending in S.
4549.srule: Non-final syllables carry one of two lesser degrees, determined by syllable structure, not by position: a full syllable CV(C)ᵀ (open or closed, with tone) is weakly stressed (W, marked ˌ); a short open presyllable CVᵀ (tone 2 or 3, e.g. ka-, ta-, sa-, la-) is unstressed (U). Either may occupy the first or the penultimate position (§3.3.2, p. 70). No positional or rhythmic secondary stress is described.

4552.prule: Tone language: lexical H vs toneless (each tone type with a lexical and a grammatical subtype) plus L 'depression' domains sponsored by breathy consonants. No plain word-stress rule is stated. Donnelly says it is only 'superficially clear that Phuthi lacks stressed syllables' and analyses prominence as 'composite, distributed and paradigm-sensitive': a right-aligned syllabic trochee at the word edge (ALIGN-WD-RT, RHTYPE=T, STRESS-TO-WEIGHT) whose head, the penult, is 'the stressed position' and is made heavy, but that redundant penult length surfaces only in phrase-final (declarative) words and is revoked phrase-medially; lexical H tone is repelled from the long penult (AVOID_PROMINENCE) and aligns to the antepenult phrase-finally, to the penult phrase-medially, and to penult or ultima in grammatical paradigms. The prominence position is thus defined by tone alignment and phrase-final length, not by a single quantity-insensitive word-stress position.

4557.dq: Apart from word stress, sentence intonation may also apply to some words such that they are pronounced with a higher pitch (see chapter 8 for details on sentence types). This is typified for instance with the focusing particles nao and ya.
4557.dloc: Beimers 2008, §3.9.2.3 'Focus particle Intonation', p. 56 (first sentence of the subsection, directly after §3.9.2.2 Stress on p. 55)
4557.prule: Word stress is lexically determined and not predictable from syllable count or weight: each word keeps stress on the syllable that bore it in its etymon (English or a Solomons vernacular), and the stressed syllable retains stress even when epenthesis (klaem ~ kalaem) or word-final paragoge (skul ~ sukulu) adds syllables; stress is never contrastive. Beimers explicitly treats the earlier fixed-penultimate (Bugotu 1972:27) and fixed-initial (Simons & Young 1978:18) accounts as partial truths subsumed by the lexical account.
4557.srule: Not mentioned in Beimers 2008 (section 3.9.2.2 'Stress', pp. 54-56 read in full; whole text consulted): the grammar places only the single word stress and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stresses.
4557.quote: Various analyses of Pijin have provided different accounts of the stress pattern of Pijin words. Bugotu (1972, p.27) says “Stress in Pidgin English, as is true in most Melanesian native tongues, usually falls on the penultimate syllable.” The account by Simons and Young (1978, p.18) says that “stress normally falls on the first syllable of Pijin words (although there are, of course, a few exceptions).” In saying that, they allow that epenthetic vowels in consonant clusters do not cause stress to shift to any new first syllable created by epenthesis.
